article_title: Detecting Knowledge Gaps from Conversational AI Interactions Using Curriculum Prerequisite Graphs
citation: Youssef Medhat, Junsoo Park, Ploy Thajchayapong and Ashok K. Goel. (2026). Detecting Knowledge Gaps from Conversational AI Interactions Using Curriculum Prerequisite Graphs. CSEDM'26: 10th Workshop on Computer Science Educational Data Mining. https://dilab.gatech.edu
title: GPT-4-extracted curriculum prerequisite knowledge graph (54 topic nodes, 47 directed prerequisite edges)
description: A prerequisite knowledge graph extracted by GPT-4 from 26 lesson PDFs of a graduate-level AI course, following a three-stage protocol of topic extraction, boundary consolidation, and edge extraction. The graph contains "54 topic nodes and 47 directed prerequisite edges" and serves two roles: its topic nodes provide the closed label space for classification and survey alignment, and its directed prerequisite edges encode curriculum structure for future per-student gap propagation. The authors describe it as "a low-cost, instructor-auditable way to obtain a topic–edge artifact".
requirements: A course instructor with domain expertise to run and audit the GPT-4 extraction protocol over lesson PDFs
constraints: The authors do not claim the graph is the unique correct structure; only unambiguous, non-bidirectional GPT-4 prerequisite judgments are retained
target_learners: graduate-level AI course students
target_learning_goals: mapping student questions to curriculum topics
identifying topic-level knowledge gaps
examples: Sample extracted edges include Semantic Networks → Frames, Case-Based Reasoning → Analogical Reasoning, and Logic → Explanation-Based Learning, matching the course textbook's lesson ordering
key_sources: Youssef Medhat, Junsoo Park, Ploy Thajchayapong and Ashok K. Goel. (2026). Detecting Knowledge Gaps from Conversational AI Interactions Using Curriculum Prerequisite Graphs. CSEDM'26: 10th Workshop on Computer Science Educational Data Mining. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.10736

title: LLM-based talk-move annotation pipeline using GPT-5.1 with a multi-theoretic codebook
description: The article describes an LLM-based measurement pipeline in which classroom recordings are transcribed by automated speech recognition with human cleanup, then annotated by GPT-5.1. "We used GPT-5.1 to annotate the transcripts chosen for the student member checks." The model was prompted with code definitions and three positive examples and three non-examples per code, assigning each sentence-level utterance binary labels for topic codes (Off-task, Recording, Competent, Understanding, Tool) and talk-move codes (Question, Apology, Claim, Reasoning, Next Step, Monitor, Disagree, Agree, Compare, Add-On, Revoice).
requirements: A human-expert-annotated validation set
Code definitions developed with human experts
Prompting with code definitions and worked examples per code
constraints: The article reports low F1 for some features, most notably Next-Step and Disagree, even after definition updates
target_learners: middle school math students in multilingual classrooms
target_learning_goals: measuring collaborative and academic talk moves in student discourse
examples: GPT-5.1 was selected over Claude 3.7 and GPT 5.0 based on F1 scores against the validation set

article_title: Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics
citation: Bastani Hamsa, Bastani Osbert, Sungu Alp, Ge Haosen, Kabakcı Özge, Mariman Rei. (2025). Generative AI without guardrails can harm learning: Evidence from high school mathematics. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America. https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2422633122
title: GPT Tutor: a guardrailed GPT-4 math tutor that gives teacher-designed hints instead of answers
description: GPT Tutor is a GPT-4 chat interface whose system prompt implements safeguards: it is instructed to "provide hints to the student without directly giving them the answer, to encourage learning", and it receives problem-specific teacher inputs including correct solutions, common student mistakes, and feedback guidance. This prevents hallucinated answers and makes the tool hard to use as a crutch. Students do not see the system prompts.
requirements: Problem-specific teacher inputs (solutions, common mistakes, hints) must be prepared for each practice problem, which the article notes is labor-intensive.
constraints: The article notes GPT Tutor remains passive, responding to questions rather than proactively engaging students with the material.
target_learners: High school mathematics students (grades 9-11)
target_learning_goals: Review and mastery of previously covered mathematics topics
examples: Deployed in four 90-minute sessions across about fifty 9th-11th grade classes in a Turkish high school, with students solving teacher-designed practice problems.

article_title: AI-generated feedback on writing: insights into efficacy and ENL student preference
citation: Escalante, J., Pack, A., & Barrett, A. (2023). AI-generated feedback on writing: insights into efficacy and ENL student preference. International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education, 20:57. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-023-00425-2
title: Role-based GPT-4 prompt for six-area corrective writing feedback
description: A structured prompt, developed iteratively by two experienced language educators, that casts GPT-4 as "a professional language teacher who is an expert on providing feedback on the writing of English language learners". It instructs the model, using simple language, to comment on six areas: topic sentence, development of ideas, language lowering academic quality, transitional phrases, use of sources and evidence, and grammatical accuracy, with grammar feedback organized into a four-column error table (sentence, error type, description, suggestion). A teaching assistant ran the prompt per student and emailed feedback within two working days.
requirements: Prompt engineering following the framework of Ingley and Pack (2023); de-identified student drafts; GPT-4 access
constraints: GPT-4 is not optimized for AWE purposes, so features like text annotation common in existing AWE programs are cumbersome to reproduce
target_learners: ENL university students writing 300-word academic paragraphs
target_learning_goals: Formative corrective feedback on academic paragraph writing
examples: Appendix B prints the full sample prompt; Appendix C shows example feedback on a student paragraph about culture, including a grammar error table

citation: Debby R. E. Cotton, Peter A. Cotton & J. Reuben Shipway (2024) Chatting and cheating: Ensuring academic integrity in the era of ChatGPT, Innovations in Education and Teaching International, 61:2, 228-239. https://doi.org/10.1080/14703297.2023.2190148
title: GPT-2 Output Detector Demo as an AI-text identification tool
description: The GPT-2 Output Detector Demo is a language-analysis tool the article names as designed to analyse the language of written work and identify patterns or irregularities indicating chatbot authorship. In the authors' December 2022 trial, ten genuine student essays scored under 1% fake probability while ChatGPT essays on the same subjects scored close to 100%, and prompting changes only lowered this to around 97%.
requirements: Submitted text to analyse; works best, per the article's trial, on unmodified ChatGPT output
constraints: The article frames detection as an arms race and notes ChatGPT's ongoing training may erode detector advantage; prompting to emulate student writing only reduced scores to around 97%
target_learners: higher education students
target_learning_goals: detecting AI-generated submissions
academic integrity
examples: The authors submitted ten student essays in December 2022 and matching ChatGPT-generated essays to the detector

article_title: Conditions for Effective Learning Without Upfront Instruction: How Practice with Feedback Supports Memory, Generalization, Motivation, and Metacognition
citation: Michael W. Asher & Paulo F. Carvalho. (2026). Conditions for Effective Learning Without Upfront Instruction: How Practice with Feedback Supports Memory, Generalization, Motivation, and Metacognition. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-025-10103-6
title: GPT-4o-generated personalized explanatory feedback for open-ended practice
description: In Study 2, the explanatory feedback condition used GPT-4o to "provide immediate, tailored explanatory feedback after each practice item", evaluating open-ended responses in real time. The prompt instructed the model to state "Correct!" or "Incorrect", explain why incorrect answers were wrong, and edit the student's exact wording with the smallest possible changes into a corrected version. Manual review of all 309 AI-generated responses found the AI correctly scored 90% of correct answers and 98% of incorrect answers, with appropriate corrections 98% of the time and no hallucinations.
requirements: GPT-4o must be given a written explanation of the problem, the criteria expected in a correct answer, and sample correct and incorrect responses based on pilot work to ensure feedback accuracy.
constraints: Accuracy was validated for this study's three regression questions and judged "sufficiently accurate for our research purposes", not as a general-purpose tutoring guarantee.
target_learners: Adult online learners practicing open-ended statistics questions
target_learning_goals: Interpreting slope and intercept of a regression line
Generating correct open-ended explanations of statistical concepts
examples: For a student who wrote only that the intercept intersects the Y axis at 5.58, the AI identified the missing interpretation and supplied a corrected version stating the predicted murder rate when temperature equals zero.

article_title: Content and Quality of Comparative Tactical Game-Centered Approaches in Physical Education: A Systematic Review
citation: Ray Breed, Riki Lindsay, Aden Kittel, Michael Spittle. (2025). Content and Quality of Comparative Tactical Game-Centered Approaches in Physical Education: A Systematic Review. Review of Educational Research. https://doi.org/10.3102/00346543241227236
title: Game Performance Assessment Instrument (GPAI) as the most utilized in-game performance tool in PE
description: The GPAI is an observational tool developed and validated in 1998 specifically for PE settings, used to assess in-game performance variables such as skill execution and tactical variables (e.g., decision-making with the ball and off-ball support), with observations coded as successful/effective or unsuccessful/ineffective, typically during a game or from postgame video. The review reports that "the GPAI has become the most utilized tool to assess in-game performance (e.g., skill execution and tactical variables) in PE and sport school settings". Related tools named are the Team Sport Assessment Procedure (TSAP) and Game Performance Evaluation Tool (GPET).
requirements: Observation during a game or postgame recording, often via video
Trained coding of observed behaviours as successful or unsuccessful
constraints: The review notes some studies used modified versions without reporting reliability or validation, or used tools in settings different from those they were validated in
target_learners: Primary and secondary school physical education students
target_learning_goals: Assessing in-game skill execution and tactical decision-making
examples: Included studies applied the GPAI in small-sided games such as 3v3, 4v4, and 5v5 formats with postgame video

citation: The Dynamic Interplay Between Goal Setting, Performance, and Emotions in Self-Regulated Learning: A Computational Modeling Approach — Supplementary Materials. (2022). https://gpemodel.shinyapps.io/gpe-model/
title: A dynamic computational model of goal setting, performance, and emotions in self-regulated learning
description: The article presents a three-equation dynamic model in which goals, performance, and emotions at each time point are each computed as a baseline intercept, an autoregressive carry-over component, a goal-performance discrepancy (GPD) component, an emotions component (for goals and performance), and random error. The model relies on tasks where participants specify goals, complete a task, and report emotion valence across repeated goal-striving episodes. It is estimated hierarchically in Stan with 95% HDIs used for significance.
requirements: Tasks must allow participants to specify goals, obtain performance, and indicate the valence of their state emotions at each time point
Estimation requires a hierarchical Bayesian framework with MCMC sampling and 95% HDIs for parameter significance
constraints: The first block is not predicted because there are no prior goal levels, performances, and emotions
No constraints on the values that goal levels, performances, and emotions could take were set
target_learners: adult participants in achievement tasks
self-regulated learners
target_learning_goals: goal setting
performance self-regulation
emotional responses to goal striving
examples: Applied to an online math task in Study 1 and to multi-day self-regulated studying in Study 2

article_title: Exploring the genetic prediction of academic underachievement and overachievement
citation: Kaito Kawakami, Francesca Procopio, Kaili Rimfeld, Margherita Malanchini, Sophie von Stumm, Kathryn Asbury, Robert Plomin. (2024). Exploring the genetic prediction of academic underachievement and overachievement. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00251-9
title: GPAΔ: a continuous genomically predicted achievement discrepancy index (observed achievement minus GPS)
description: GPAΔ (Genomically-Predicted Achievement Discrepancy) is a continuous difference score created by subtracting a standardized genome-wide polygenic score (EA4, based on educational attainment) from standardized observed achievement. The authors state they "devised an index called Genomically-Predicted Achievement Discrepancy (GPAΔ) by subtracting a GPS for adult educational attainment from educational achievement at age 7." Negative scores indicate underachievement and positive scores overachievement, spanning a continuum rather than dichotomizing students. Domain-specific versions (English–GPS, Mathematics–GPS) were also constructed.
requirements: Requires genotyping and creation of a genome-wide polygenic score, plus assessed early school achievement to compute the difference
constraints: Until a GWA study is done on GPAΔ per se, GPAΔ requires that early school achievement is assessed so the difference between GPS and observed achievement can be obtained
GPS predictive power is attenuated in populations with different ancestries; the study included only participants of European ancestry
target_learners: children in the early school years (age 7)
target_learning_goals: identifying academic underachievement and overachievement for personalized educational support
examples: In the TEDS cohort, GPAΔ at age 7 was computed for 4175 genotyped participants and correlated with achievement slopes across ages 7, 9, 12, and 16
key_sources: Kaito Kawakami, Francesca Procopio, Kaili Rimfeld, Margherita Malanchini, Sophie von Stumm, Kathryn Asbury, Robert Plomin. (2024). Exploring the genetic prediction of academic underachievement and overachievement. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00251-9

article_title: Exploring the genetic prediction of academic underachievement and overachievement
citation: Kaito Kawakami, Francesca Procopio, Kaili Rimfeld, Margherita Malanchini, Sophie von Stumm, Kathryn Asbury, Robert Plomin. (2024). Exploring the genetic prediction of academic underachievement and overachievement. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-024-00251-9
title: Use genomic discrepancy indices as an early-warning system to target underachievers early, pending intervention tests
description: The article proposes GPAΔ screening as an early-warning system: because GPS are stable from conception, they can flag likely underachievers before achievement falls far behind, when interventions are most likely to succeed. The authors argue "Targeting GPAΔ underachievers might prove cost-effective because such interventions seem more likely to succeed by going with the genetic ﬂow rather than swimming upstream." This remains an explicitly untested hypothesis requiring intervention research.
requirements: Intervention research testing whether GPAΔ underachievers respond better to intervention than other underachievers
Early school achievement must be assessed to compute the GPS–achievement difference
constraints: Interventions effective for GPAΔ underachievers might be less effective in preventing the decline of GPAΔ overachievers
GPAΔ currently requires DNA, genotyping, and GPS creation; predictive power represents an upper bound for European-ancestry samples
target_learners: children in the early school years, particularly those underachieving relative to genomic prediction
target_learning_goals: early identification of underachievement to personalize education and maximize achievement toward individual potential
examples: The study screened 4175 TEDS participants at age 7 and charted trajectories showing underachievers regressing about one-third toward genomic prediction by age 16

citation: Jionghao Lin, Zifei Han, Danielle R. Thomas, Ashish Gurung, Shivang Gupta, Vincent Aleven, Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2024). How Can I Get It Right? Using GPT to Rephrase Incorrect Trainee Responses. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.00970
title: GPT-4-based explanatory feedback system for tutor training
description: An automated feedback system built on the GPT-4 model that identifies trainees' responses in binary form (correct/incorrect) and provides template-based feedback with incorrect responses rephrased by GPT-4. The system targets novice tutors in scenario-based training lessons on an online learning platform. As the authors state, "our study employed the GPT-4 model to build an explanatory feedback system", integrating the classifier and rephrasing results into real-time feedback during training sessions.
requirements: Requires a binary classifier (the 5-shot GPT-4 classifier) to pinpoint incorrect responses before rephrasing
Requires lesson-specific principles and scenario text as prompt inputs
constraints: Evaluated only on three lessons; the authors call for broader evaluation on other lessons
Binary correct/incorrect classification may be overly simplistic for real-world applications, per the authors
target_learners: novice tutors (trainees), including community volunteers, retired individuals, and college students
target_learning_goals: effective praise
reacting to student errors
determining what students know
examples: The system presents template-based suggestions such as "AI-generated feedback suggests that your response could focus more on praising the student for their efforts in the learning process."

title: Game-based physical activity plans integrating science outcomes from simple to complex across a five-week unit
description: A lesson-level design in which the outcomes of a science unit are mapped onto a sequence of game-based physical activities, integrated "from simple to complex" across five weeks. Safety outcome 4 was embedded in every plan because of the risk inherent in physical play.

citation: Prinz, M., Schäfer, E., Bürklein, S. & Donnermeyer, D. (2026) Endodontic diagnostics training in undergraduate dental education: An observational pilot study on AI‐driven virtual patient e‐learning. International Endodontic Journal, 59, 1145–1159. https://doi.org/10.1111/iej.14277
title: GPT-4-turbo-based virtual patient web app for endodontic diagnostic training
description: A web-app e-learning platform with three components: a user-facing website, a MongoDB database server holding patient case information with radiographic and clinical images, and the GPT-4-turbo model (OpenAI) accessed via API. Eight patient cases covered the most common endodontic pathologies, with diagnoses such as acute irreversible pulpitis and cracked tooth syndrome.

A universal system prompt with placeholders integrating case information from the database, instructing the model to answer only from the case information and to avoid hallucination

The model was barred from using general web information and responds "I am not sure" when case-related information is unavailable
target_learners: 4th- and 5th-year undergraduate dental students
target_learning_goals: Endodontic pain diagnostics and clinical decision-making
Patient communication and obtaining informed consent
examples: Students solved eight virtual patient cases over a 3-month individual-use period; 38.9% of participants completed all eight cases

article_title: Comparing AI chatbot simulation and peer role-play for OSCE preparation: a pilot randomized controlled trial.
citation: Lee Hye-Yoon, Kim Jundong, Choi Hyojae, Bae Hyojin, Jeong Aram, Choi Sungyoul, Kim Ji-Hwan, Kim Chang-Eop. (2025). Comparing AI chatbot simulation and peer role-play for OSCE preparation: a pilot randomized controlled trial. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-08308-y
title: Multi-layered GPT-4o/Claude 3.5 Sonnet OSCE simulation chatbot with automated scoring and text feedback
description: A proprietary educational AI chatbot combining GPT-4o and Claude 3.5 Sonnet in a multi-layered architecture, used as the experimental training tool in the pilot RCT. OSCE scenarios were "converted into chart‑style prompts optimized for SP role simulation"; the chatbot acted as a simulated patient, generated natural responses to student inquiries, and after each interview provided "both quantitative scoring and individualized text feedback based on the dialogue". Students practiced dizziness and shoulder pain cases freely without time or attempt restrictions.
requirements: Pre-designed chart-style scenario prompts; a clinical expert supervising sessions; reliable server performance and technical support on standby
constraints: Students reported inability to implement physical examination, lack of understanding of Korean medicine terminology, absence of real interaction with patients, and scoring speed delay
target_learners: final-year Korean medicine students preparing for OSCE
target_learning_goals: clinical interview and history taking
patient education
clinical reasoning
examples: In the trial, the chatbot group practiced two clinical presentations with two cases each for one hour under clinical expert supervision, submitting sessions for automated scoring and LLM-generated text feedback
key_sources: Lee Hye-Yoon, Kim Jundong, Choi Hyojae, Bae Hyojin, Jeong Aram, Choi Sungyoul, Kim Ji-Hwan, Kim Chang-Eop. (2025). article_title: The effects of video-based and blended learning on medication dosage calculation skills of paramedic students: A randomized, quasi-experimental study.
citation: Baran L, Öztürk H. (2025). The effects of video-based and blended learning on medication dosage calculation skills of paramedic students: A randomized, quasi-experimental study. Medicine 104(31):e43651. https://doi.org/10.1097/MD.0000000000043651
title: Use GPA-ranked systematic assignment to balance ability levels when randomizing students into instructional comparison groups
description: Because students with higher GPAs tend to achieve higher MDC test scores, the authors ranked all 158 consenting students by GPA and alternately assigned odd-ranked students to the BL group and even-ranked students to the VBL group. This systematic procedure controlled the GPA confound that simple randomization may leave unbalanced, while acknowledging that self-reported learning style and numerical competency are unreliable to stratify on.
requirements: Access to students' GPA records before assignment and a full cohort enrollment approach
constraints: Self-reported numerical competency and learning style may be inaccurate, limiting stratification on those variables
target_learners: Undergraduate health-program students participating in instructional comparison studies
target_learning_goals: Fair comparison of instructional methods on skills outcomes such as medication dosage calculation
examples: The study verified no significant GPA difference between groups (t = −1.48, P = .140) after ranked assignment

title: GPT-4–powered virtual simulated patient platform for practicing abnormal mammogram result conversations
description: A virtual training module built in Hyperskill (SimInsights) simulation authoring software, using automated speech recognition and text-to-speech for real-time spoken conversation with a GPT-4–driven virtual simulated patient. The final scenario flow "consisted of only 2 states (setup and feedback)", with the AI chatbot generating patient replies in real time and an AI feedback agent producing postconversation assessment with quoted examples. Medical students role-play a PCP telephoning the patient about abnormal diagnostic mammogram results requiring a biopsy.
requirements: A detailed text prompt specifying scenario context, patient emotional state, and expected responses to learner choices, iteratively refined through agile testing cycles
constraints: VSP dialogue and generated feedback are not standardized, so the authors state it is unlikely the training could currently be used in summative clinical examinations
target_learners: medical students
target_learning_goals: communicating abnormal mammogram results with patients
adhering to the SPIKES protocol for delivering difficult news
empathic patient-centered communication
examples: The scenario simulates a telephone call, depicted as a 3D cell phone on a physician's desk with a red End button that ends the conversation and triggers feedback generation.

article_title: Evaluating general practitioners' focused lung ultrasound competence and findings in patients with suspected community-acquired pneumonia in general practice.
citation: Strøm, J. J., Andersen, C. A., Jensen, M. B., Thomsen, J. L., Laursen, C. B., Skaarup, S. H., Schultz, H. H. L., & Hansen, M. P. (2025). Evaluating general practitioners' focused lung ultrasound competence and findings in patients with suspected community-acquired pneumonia in general practice. Scandinavian Journal of Primary Health Care, 43(2), 359-369. https://doi.org/10.1080/02813432.2024.2447083
title: Tailored three-component FLUS training program for general practitioners (theoretical self-study with validated MCQ test, one-day hands-on course with LUS-OSAUS assessment, and supervised real-life scans)
description: The training program prepared GPs to learn the indications for FLUS, execute the validated 14-zone FLUS protocol, and interpret findings. It "consisted of" theoretical self-study concluding with a validated multiple-choice test (pass cut-off score 20 of 0-30), a one-day hands-on course completing with a practical LUS-OSAUS assessment under standardised conditions, and five to ten FLUS scans in the GP's clinic supervised remotely by respiratory-medicine FLUS specialists at EFSUMB level III competence. Its content aligned with Danish and European Respiratory Society FLUS training courses.
requirements: Participants must pass the theoretical MCQ test at a cut-off score of 20 (range 0-30) and complete a practical LUS-OSAUS assessment, plus five to ten remotely supervised FLUS scans within one month of the hands-on course.
constraints: The study evaluated the program only in nine GPs who were already POCUS users, so generalizability to a broader GP population is uncertain.
target_learners: general practitioners using point-of-care ultrasound
target_learning_goals: learn indications for performing FLUS
execute the 14-zone FLUS protocol
interpret FLUS findings
examples: Nine GPs completed the program with MCQ-test scores between 20-26 (median = 25) and LUS-OSAUS scores of 96-100% of maximum (median = 99%).

citation: Zhang Yuqin, Sun Xuemei, Zhong Wen, Sun Dingkui, Gao Yingyan, Chen Xiyang, Zhang Weiru. (2025). BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2024-094404
title: General Practitioners' Ability to Identify and Manage Depression assessment scale
description: A 24-item self-assessment scale with two dimensions, recognition (10 items) and management (14 items), measuring general practitioners' competence in recognising and managing depression in primary care. Each item is rated on a five-point Likert scale from 'completely unable' to 'completely able', and 'a total score is calculated, where a higher score reflects greater recognition and management capabilities'. The article describes it as 'straightforward' and resource-efficient compared with standardised-patient or psychiatrist re-evaluation methods.
requirements: Completed anonymously by GPs working primarily in community or primary care settings, based on their self-assessed ability to recognise and manage depression
constraints: The study did not include a direct comparison with other scales
Further validation in more diverse regions is needed to improve the scale's general applicability
target_learners: General practitioners in Chinese primary healthcare
target_learning_goals: Recognition of depression
Management of depression in primary care
examples: Administered online via Wenjuanxin questionnaires distributed through WeChat groups and academic forums between 2023 and 2024 across four development phases

article_title: Developing a professional competency framework for general practitioners in tertiary hospitals in China: a modified Delphi study.
citation: Wei Yun, An Yanhua, Cao Qiumei, Feng Wei, Wang Dawei, Zhu Dan. (2025). Developing a professional competency framework for general practitioners in tertiary hospitals in China: a modified Delphi study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2023-082736
title: Professional competency framework for GPs in tertiary hospitals in China (4 primary, 12 secondary, 54 tertiary indicators)
description: A three-level professional competency framework for general practitioners in Chinese tertiary hospitals, developed via a modified Delphi process. It organises competency into four primary domains — medical services, teaching, research and prevention — with the final structure including "4 primary indicators, 12 secondary indicators and 54 tertiary indicators". It is intended for use in medical education, general practice research, quality improvement, GP self-evaluation and multisource feedback.
requirements: Consensus criteria: median score exceeding seven on a 9-point scale and at least 70% of panel ratings in the top tertile (7–9) for both importance and feasibility
constraints: The results may have limited generalisability due to expert selection
The effectiveness of the competency framework in real practice settings is unknown
target_learners: General practitioners in tertiary hospitals in China
GP residency trainees in tertiary hospital general practice departments
target_learning_goals: Professional competency assessment of GPs in tertiary hospitals
Competency feedback for GPs in China
examples: Two rounds of email Delphi surveys from August to October 2022 with 19 experts
Initial framework of 4 primary, 14 secondary and 48 tertiary indicators derived from a literature review of 31 published papers and three policy documents

article_title: How is self-regulated learning documented in e-portfolios of trainees? A content analysis.
citation: van der Gulden R, Heeneman S, Kramer AWM, Laan RFJM, Scherpbier-de Haan ND, Thoonen BPA. (2020). How is self-regulated learning documented in e-portfolios of trainees? A content analysis. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-020-02114-4
title: Dutch GP training e-portfolio with eleven pre-structured forms designed to combine programmatic assessment with SRL support
description: The e-portfolio used in Dutch GP specialty training contains eleven unique pre-structured forms (e.g. Compass, Mini-CEX, learning goals and plans, request for feedback) that can be added as often as required, plus a separate folder for trainees' own documents. Its "Content and structure of the e-portfolio are based on the research-informed NijMaas guidelines", whose "mission ... was to propose an e-portfolio that combines programmatic assessment with support for SRL". Each form was labelled at design time with the SRL processes it was envisioned to support.
requirements: Trainees are obligated to document assessment and learning information in the e-portfolio, which is shared with teachers, supervisors and heads of the GP Training Institute
constraints: The folder containing personal documents could not be anonymised, so the study covered only the pre-structured forms
target_learners: GP trainees in the Dutch three-year General Practitioner specialty training
target_learning_goals: Self-regulated learning processes: self-assessment via reflection and feedback, goal-setting and planning, and monitoring
examples: The study analysed a mirror database of 1022 anonymous e-portfolios from three institutes, covering 2013 to March 2018

article_title: Effect of a dementia education intervention on the confidence and attitudes of general practitioners in Australia: a pretest post-test study.
citation: Mason Ron, Doherty Kathleen, Eccleston Claire, Winbolt Margaret, Long Marita, Robinson Andrew. (2020). Effect of a dementia education intervention on the confidence and attitudes of general practitioners in Australia: a pretest post-test study. BMJ Open. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmjopen-2019-033218
title: GPACS-D: General Practitioners Confidence and Attitude Scale for Dementia
description: The GPACS-D is a validated survey instrument for measuring GPs' confidence and attitudes towards dementia before and after targeted education. The article states "The GPACS-D comprises three subscales: Confidence in Clinical Abilities (six items), Attitude to Care (six items) and Engagement (three items)", validated using confirmatory factor analysis. It employs a Likert scale scored from 1 (strongly agree) to 5 (strongly disagree), with subscale scores standardised to a minimum of 1 and maximum of 5 so subscales can be compared. In this study a research assistant not associated with workshop delivery administered it immediately before (T1) and after (T2) each workshop.
requirements: Administered as matched pre and post surveys, with each presurvey and postsurvey matched via a unique ID for each attendee.
constraints: The article notes the survey did not fully capture attitudes towards disclosure or perceived self-efficacy regarding communication.
target_learners: General practitioner registrars
General practitioner supervisors
target_learning_goals: Confidence in dementia diagnosis and management
Attitudes towards dementia care
Engagement with people with dementia
examples: Used as the outcome measure for 332 registrars and 114 supervisors in the pretest post-test evaluation of the dementia workshops.

article_title: Using simulation to explore medical students' understanding of integrated care within geriatrics.
citation: Yang S, Chaudhary Z, Mylopoulos M, Hashmi R, Kwok Y, Colman S, Yogaparan T, Sockalingam S. (2019). Using simulation to explore medical students' understanding of integrated care within geriatrics. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-019-1758-9
title: GPS-Care (Getting to Know Patients' System of Care) interprofessional simulation
description: GPS-Care is a simulation in which "medical students role-playing a geriatric patient or one of their two caregivers navigating through a simulated healthcare system". In groups of three, students attend five simulated appointments with a geriatric nurse, psychiatrist or psychologist, occupational therapist, social worker, and community pharmacist, with primary care physician follow-up between appointments. The 1.5-hour experience concludes with a 45-min facilitator-led group debrief, followed by a written reflection.
requirements: Five patient and caregiver scenario stems developed by content experts and clinician reviewers
A 15 min orientation session before stations
A facilitator-led 45-min debrief session after the experience
constraints: Implemented at a single institution (University of Toronto) as part of a mandatory two-year training program
target_learners: first-year undergraduate medical students
target_learning_goals: understanding of integrated care for patients with co-occurring physical and mental health needs
patient and caregiver perspectives on navigating the healthcare system
examples: 177 of 259 first-year medical students participated; students completed written reflections and 7 students gave one-on-one interviews

article_title: The effect of small-sided games with different levels of opposition on the tactical behaviour of young footballers with different levels of sport expertise.
citation: Práxedes A, Moreno A, Gil-Arias A, Claver F, Del Villar F. (2018). The effect of small-sided games with different levels of opposition on the tactical behaviour of young footballers with different levels of sport expertise. PLoS ONE 13(1): e0190157. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0190157
title: GPET (Game Performance Evaluation Tool) for observing decision-making and execution in real matches
description: The GPET is an observation instrument, an adaptation to football of the Game Performance Assessment Instrument (GPAI), used "to assess the decision-making and execution of football players" in real game situations. Decision-making is coded 1 for appropriate and 0 for inappropriate choices (e.g. passing to an unmarked teammate vs a marked one), and execution 1 for successful passes (appropriate length and speed) and 0 for unsuccessful ones (interception, out of play). Percentages of successful decisions and executions are computed per player. In this study it was applied to 4901 passes across 20 league matches with inter-observer reliability above .90.
requirements: Trained observers with reliability above the .81 adequacy threshold
Recorded video of matches from a fixed elevated camera position
target_learners: youth team-sport players assessed in real match play
target_learning_goals: measuring tactical decision-making and skill execution as learning outcomes
examples: All pass actions of each player were coded in league matches; 510 passes (more than 10% of the total) were double-coded for reliability, with Cohen kappa values above .90 and intraobserver reliability of .92.

article_title: A Multi-Gene Genetic Programming Application for Predicting Students Failure at School
citation: J.O. Orove, N.E. Osegi, B.O. Eke. (2013). A Multi-Gene Genetic Programming Application for Predicting Students Failure at School. https://www.osegi.com
title: GPSFARPS: a multi-gene genetic programming software application for predicting student failure rate at school
description: GPSFARPS is a software application built on the open-source GPTIPS framework that evolves model expressions for predicting student failure rate from historical class/exam score data. The article states it was developed "to provide a robust solution to the prediction of SFR using an evolutionary algorithm known as multi-gene genetic programming". It consists of three core windows (Start, Main, Grammar) for data entry, GP parameter specification, and failure-rate classification, and its evolved expressions can be reused by school administrators on future data sets.
requirements: A historical data set of student raw scores (predictor variables Q1-Q5 and CA score, response variable TOTAL) and a system configuration file must be fed to the GP system
constraints: The system was fed incomplete raw score data in the reported simulation
The application is built within a scripting program using MATLAB handle graphics
target_learners: school students whose failure rate administrators want to predict
target_learning_goals: predicting student failure rate to support curricula and teaching-system evaluation
examples: The application was trained on sample raw score data (Table 1) with GP parameters of population size 150, 500 generations, tournament size 4, and maximum tree depth 4

article_title: Elucidating STEM Concepts through Generative AI: A Multi-modal Exploration of Analogical Reasoning
citation: Cao, C., Ding, Z., Lee, G.-G., Jiao, J., Lin, J., & Zhai, X. (2023). Elucidating STEM Concepts through Generative AI: A Multi-modal Exploration of Analogical Reasoning. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.10454
title: AI-driven multimodal analogy generation prototype for STEM concepts
description: The article describes a prototype backed by GPT-4 that generates analogies for STEM concepts and transforms them into visual media. Users input a concept such as "Newton's first Law" and the model generates three distinct analogies, which are converted via preset prompts into a four-image storyboard and then an animated video. The tool is deployed live at the article's printed URL.
requirements: Users provide a STEM concept as input and select a preferred analogy before storyboard generation
constraints: Content generation for multi-component STEM concepts was incomplete in preliminary testing
target_learners: STEM learners, particularly novices learning programming, physics, and mathematics
target_learning_goals: comprehension of abstract STEM concepts such as algorithms, physical laws, and programming constructs
examples: For Object-Oriented Programming, objects were analogized as Lego bricks and classes were likened to structures of Lego

article_title: Ruffle&Riley: Towards the Automated Induction of Conversational Tutoring Systems
citation: Robin Schmucker, Meng Xia, Amos Azaria, Tom Mitchell. (2023). Ruffle&Riley: Towards the Automated Induction of Conversational Tutoring Systems. NeurIPS'23 Workshop on Generative AI for Education (GAIED). https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01420
title: Four-step GPT4 pipeline for automatic tutoring script induction from lesson text
description: The article describes an automated authoring pipeline in which GPT4 induces an expectation-misconception-tailoring (EMT) style tutoring script directly from a lesson text. It prints that "This involves a 4-step process: (i) A list of review questions is generated from the lesson text; (ii) For each question, a solution is generated based on question and lesson texts", followed by expectation generation and compilation of the script as questions with related expectations. Unlike traditional EMT-based CTSs, the scripts do not anticipate misconceptions ahead of time; instead the system relies on GPT4 detecting factually incorrect information in learner responses during teaching.
requirements: Three separate prompts written generally enough to support a wide range of lesson materials, and a lesson text as source material
constraints: The scripts do not attempt to anticipate misconceptions learners might exhibit ahead of time, which the authors call a difficult task even for human domain experts
target_learners: instructional designers and educators seeking to author CTS content without labor-intensive configuration
target_learning_goals: automated generation of questions, solutions and expectations for conversational tutoring across lesson domains
examples: The pipeline was applied to a Biology lesson on organelles of eukaryotic cells adapted from the OpenStax project
key_sources: Robin Schmucker, Meng Xia, Amos Azaria, Tom Mitchell. (2023). Ruffle&Riley: Towards the Automated Induction of Conversational Tutoring Systems. NeurIPS'23 Workshop on Generative AI for Education (GAIED). https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.01420

adult crowdworkers

article_title: Reforming Physics Exams Using Openly Accessible Large Isomorphic Problem Banks created with the assistance of Generative AI: an Explorative Study
citation: Zhongzhou Chen, Emily Frederick, Colleen Cui, Munaimah Khan, Christopher Klatt, Mercedith Huang, Shiyang Su. (2023). Reforming Physics Exams Using Openly Accessible Large Isomorphic Problem Banks created with the assistance of Generative AI: an Explorative Study. https://platform.openai.com/playground
title: A five-step generative-AI-assisted procedure for creating isomorphic problem banks using GPT-3, Inkscape and Wolfram Alpha
description: The article describes a five-step workflow for building isomorphic problem banks: a human expert writes and reviews a seed problem; experts decide acceptable isomorphic variations at three hierarchical levels; SVG figures are created and edited with the free open-source tool Inkscape; GPT-3 in completion mode generates problem text via one-shot and few-shot prompting; and Wolfram Alpha computes correct symbolic or numeric answers. The article reports that "The estimated cost for generating all the problem text used in this study is less than $1", and that all created problems are stored in a JSON file format and uploaded to a Github repository.
requirements: Human content experts write and review the seed problem and decide which variations are acceptable as isomorphic
Access to GPT-3, Inkscape, and Wolfram Alpha, with problems stored in a JSON file format
constraints: The procedure requires significantly more human input at every step than fully automatic generation attempts, which the authors argue reduces LLM hallucination errors and enables correction of biases
target_learners: college introductory-level calculus-based physics students
target_learning_goals: assessing problem-solving on targeted physics learning outcomes such as static friction and energy conservation
examples: Three banks were created in Spring 2023: Static Friction with 24 total problems, Energy Conservation with 44, and Ballistic Pendulum with 45

article_title: Exploring Generative AI assisted feedback writing for students' written responses to a physics conceptual question with prompt engineering and few-shot learning
citation: Tong Wan and Zhongzhou Chen. (2023). Exploring Generative AI assisted feedback writing for students' written responses to a physics conceptual question with prompt engineering and few-shot learning. https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.02662
title: GPT-3.5-turbo grading assistant for feedback on free-response physics conceptual questions
description: A generative AI grading assistant configuration in which GPT-3.5-turbo in complete mode, accessed through Azure OpenAI Studio, generates feedback to student written responses given a prompt containing context, the physics problem, an expert response, physics principles, feedback instructions, and few-shot examples. The article demonstrates "the feasibility of using Generative AI as an assistant to generate feedback for student written responses with only a relatively small number of examples in the prompt."
requirements: A small number of instructor-written response-feedback example pairs included in the prompt
A stop sequence setting so the model generates only the feedback text
constraints: Evaluated on only one conceptual question with a relatively small number of student responses
The feedback design directly hints at Newtonian reasoning rather than building on students' existing ideas, since multi-round dialogue is significantly more complicated to develop and out of scope
target_learners: introductory physics students in studio-mode courses
target_learning_goals: articulating reasoning and justifying conclusions on free-response conceptual questions about Newton's second and third laws
examples: The study used 85 student responses to a Maryland Open Source Tutorial question about whether a 200 N force is transmitted to box B, generating feedback for 16 responses in stage one and 65 in stage three.

title: GPT-3.5 Turbo AI grading pipeline with three prompt versions (Naive, Detailed-rubric, Scaffolded COT)
description: The system is a GPT-3.5 Turbo deployment in completion mode, accessed via the Microsoft Azure platform through the LangChain AzureOpenAI python API, with all data kept on university-owned secure servers. The article develops and tests three prompt versions — "Naïve COT", "Detailed-rubric COT", and "Scaffolded COT" — each with identical contextual information, general grading instructions, and problem statement components but different rubric and grading-requirement components. It grades student explanations on a three-item binary rubric for a water-slide conceptual question.
requirements: Rubric items with binary 1/0 ratings, evaluated on percent agreement, mean simple matching distance, and quadratic weighted kappa against human raters
constraints: The study tested one physics conceptual problem and only explanations from students who answered the multiple-choice question incorrectly (N = 40)
target_learners: undergraduate students in a 99-enrollment calculus-based introductory physics course
target_learning_goals: automated partial-credit grading of written explanations to reduce instructor and teaching-assistant grading load in large-enrollment courses
examples: On a midterm exam, students were told wrong multiple-choice answers would earn partial credit according to their explanation of their reasoning

article_title: Comparing student performance on a multi-attempt asynchronous assessment to a single-attempt synchronous assessment in introductory level physics
citation: Emily Frederick and Zhongzhou Chen. (2024). Comparing student performance on a multi-attempt asynchronous assessment to a single-attempt synchronous assessment in introductory level physics. arXiv:2407.15257 [physics.ed-ph]. https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.15257
title: GPT-3.5-generated isomorphic problem banks with human specialist review
description: The study used large isomorphic problem banks generated with the assistance of the large language model GPT-3.5 and uploaded to the Canvas learning management platform. The banks contained 44 variations of a numerical ballistic-pendulum problem and 21 variations of a conceptual multiple-answer problem. The authors "define isomorphic problems as problems that tests the same set of learning objectives". Generation proceeded by selecting a seed problem, defining viable isomorphic variations, and prompting GPT-3.5 one problem at a time.
requirements: Each generated problem was reviewed and edited by a human specialist to ensure validity before upload to the learning management platform
constraints: The numerical bank contained 44 variations and the conceptual bank 21 variations, as printed in the method section
target_learners: undergraduate students in a calculus-based introductory physics course
target_learning_goals: conservation of linear momentum
conservation of mechanical energy
examples: The numerical bank's variations were isomorphic to the ballistic pendulum problem, with minor variations replacing bullets and pendulum with carts or boxes and major variations replacing the pendulum with an ideal spring

article_title: Evaluating the capability of large language models to personalize science texts for diverse middle-school-age learners
citation: Vaccaro Jr., M., Friday, M., and Zaghi, A. (2024). Evaluating the capability of large language models to personalize science texts for diverse middle-school-age learners. https://github.com/m-vaccaro/LLMs-and-Personalized-Learning
title: GPT-4 profiler-and-rewrite pipeline for personalizing science texts
description: A two-model GPT-4 pipeline (version gpt-4-1106-preview) in which a "profiler" model converts a student's four training-session paragraph choices into a short learning-preference profile, and a "rewrite" model uses that profile to personalize an educational science text. The study's GUI implemented the procedure for both experimental and control groups, with the control group's rewrite model taking the opposite profile as input. The system and user prompts defining both models were developed in a prior simulation study and released on the authors' GitHub page.
requirements: Training-session choice data from the student, engineered system and user prompts for both models, and source texts on middle-school science topics
constraints: The profile was limited to the Felder-Silverman model's four dimensions and remained static during the experiment, based only on the four training-session choices
target_learners: seventh- and eighth-grade middle school students (ages 11-13)
target_learning_goals: reading and comprehending middle-school science texts (water cycle, climate change, photosynthesis, states of matter, plate tectonics, electricity)
examples: Twelve experimental-group students received texts rewritten from their true profile; eleven control-group students received texts rewritten from the opposite profile, and both groups chose between personalized and generic paragraphs

article_title: Assessing GPTZero's Accuracy in Identifying AI vs. Human-Written Essays
citation: Selin Dik, Osman Erdem, and Mehmet Dik. (2024). Assessing GPTZero's Accuracy in Identifying AI vs. Human-Written Essays.
title: 78-essay GPTZero test corpus of human-written and ChatGPT-generated essays across three length categories
description: The study assembled a corpus of "fifty human written essays and twenty-eight AI written essays", with human essays written without AI help and AI essays generated from random prompts using ChatGPT. Essays were sorted into short (under 100 words), medium (100-350 words), and long (over 350 words) categories, then each was copied and pasted into GPTZero, which returned a percentage chance the essay was AI-written. Averages were computed for six human/AI by length categories.
requirements: Essays must be individually submitted to GPTZero with word count recorded alongside the returned AI-generation percentage for later category averaging.
constraints: The corpus covers word counts between forty and eight hundred words and uses only ChatGPT-generated AI text; the authors note future work should include mixed human-and-AI texts and other factors such as page count or font size.
target_learners: students whose essays were used as the human-written sample
target_learning_goals: evaluating the reliability of AI writing detectors used in academic settings
examples: The six resulting categories were short, medium, and long essays written by humans, and short, medium, and long essays written by AI.

article_title: Students' Perceptions to a Large Language Model's Generated Feedback and Scores of Argumentation Essays
citation: Winter Allen, Anand Shanker, N. Sanjay Rebello. (2025). Students' Perceptions to a Large Language Model's Generated Feedback and Scores of Argumentation Essays. arXiv preprint. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14759
title: GPT-4o pipeline for scoring and feedback on written physics arguments
description: The article describes a feedback-generation pipeline in which "Student responses were downloaded from our Learning Management System (LMS) and given to OpenAI's GPT 4o [55] using its application programming interface (API)." The API was fed the problem, an example of an ideal answer, and a 5-point rubric emphasizing claims centered on the appropriate physics principle and appropriate evidence, with temperature set to 0.80. Students received their score and feedback via a tiny URL, and the rubrics mirrored the recitation scaffolding.
requirements: An LMS export of student responses, API access to GPT-4o, a rubric, an example ideal answer, and a prompt constraining feedback to physics content.
constraints: In this study the feedback was delayed: students received it only at the end of the semester and only for three quizzes, so there was likely little benefit to the progression of student written argumentation.
target_learners: students in large-enrollment introductory physics courses
target_learning_goals: improving written scientific argumentation
metacognitive reflection on problem-solving strategies
examples: One student who received a score of 3 out of 5 found the feedback extremely useful and mostly accurate; the example feedback noted the essay mentioned the extended system energy principle but not the point particle energy principle.

article_title: Using an LLM to Investigate Students' Explanations on Conceptual Physics Questions
citation: Sean Savage, N. Sanjay Rebello. (2025). Using an LLM to Investigate Students’ Explanations on Conceptual Physics Questions. https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14823
title: GPT-4o grading-and-categorization pipeline for written physics explanations
description: A Jupyter-Notebook pipeline calls OpenAI's GPT-4o API to grade students' written claim-evidence-reasoning responses to three EMCS questions, one question at a time. The prompt combines role prompting ("...experienced physics educator...") with chain-of-thought scoring ("Before assigning scores, think through the student’s response step by step"), outputs a .csv with claim, evidence/reasoning, and overall correctness flags, and generates emergent categories.
requirements: Students must produce written claim-evidence-reasoning responses; the article notes students had received considerable instruction in the framework in the recitation component of the course
constraints: The study covered only three of 25 EMCS questions due to concern for student fatigue
The LLM was less likely to mark a student as completely correct than the human grader
target_learners: first-semester calculus-based physics undergraduates in large-enrollment courses (N > 1,000)
target_learning_goals: assessing conceptual understanding of energy and momentum, including students' written explanations and conceptual resources
examples: Q05, Q16, and Q23 post-test responses were graded with average fully-correct rates of 33 ± 1.1%, 27 ± 1.6%, and 45 ± 0.7% across three LLM runs

article_title: One-Topic-Doesn't-Fit-All: Transcreating Reading Comprehension Test for Personalized Learning
citation: Jieun Han, Daniel Lee, Haneul Yoo, Jinsung Yoon, Junyeong Park, Suin Kim, So-Yeon Ahn, Alice Oh. (2025). One-Topic-Doesn't-Fit-All: Transcreating Reading Comprehension Test for Personalized Learning. arXiv. https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.09135
title: Five-step personalized transcreation pipeline using gpt-4o
description: A systematic pipeline that adapts RACE-C reading passages and multiple-choice questions to individual students' interests using "LLM-driven transcreation" with gpt-4o under an English teacher system prompt. It has five steps: topic extraction into nine categories and 33 subcategories from Korea's curriculum; question classification into six Bloom's taxonomy categories; extraction of key linguistic features using 41 special tags; reading passage transcreation preserving those features; and question transcreation maintaining the original cognitive demands.
requirements: An English teacher system prompt for pedagogical quality
The RACE-C dataset as the source of passages and questions
Collection of individual students' interests to target transcreation
constraints: 2.8% of transcreated questions were deemed unanswerable due to LLM temporal reasoning limits and required expert modification
target_learners: EFL learners in South Korea
college-level English reading students
target_learning_goals: English reading comprehension
sustained engagement and motivation in reading
examples: A RACE-C passage about senior citizen discounts was transcreated into a passage about online versus offline education, keeping the conjunction linguistic feature and the Remember-level Bloom's question type

description: GPTutor is an LLM-powered tutoring system for undergraduate discrete mathematics that integrates "a structured proof-review tool and a conversational chatbot." The proof-review component provides high-level feedback and localized comments highlighting specific problematic segments, supports only structured feedback without open-ended dialogue, and requires students to produce a proof attempt before receiving feedback. gifted high-school and elementary pupils reached through outreach

preparation for scientific careers and diverse employment paths

article_title: Performance of GPT-4o combined with retrieval-augmented generation on nutritionist licensing exam questions.
citation: Ishikawa Yu, Higashi Akitaka, Arai Nozomu, Ozo Daisuke, Hasegawa Wataru, Imamura Tetsuya, Matsumoto Zenbei, Nambo Hidetaka, Karashima Shigehiro. (2025). description: A retrieval-augmented generation system built by integrating GPT-4o with a custom three-step pipeline: knowledge base construction (documents related to nutrition counseling collected, vectorized, and indexed in a searchable database), document retrieval (cosine similarity scores identify and retrieve the most relevant documents for each query), and answer generation (retrieved documents combined with the input query into a prompt processed by GPT). The knowledge base used publicly available documents from professional academic societies and government-issued guidelines. The system was evaluated on national dietitian examination questions and a counseling simulation.

patients receiving nutrition counseling

nutrition knowledge assessment
clinical nutrition decision support

article_title: Fine-tuning with RAG for Improving LLM Learning of New Skills
citation: Humaid Ibrahim, Nikolai Rozanov, Marek Rei. (2025). Fine-Tuning with RAG for Improving LLM Learning of New Skills. ICLR 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01375
title: Failure-driven hint extraction method using GPT-4o
description: An automatic method to generate typed, reusable guidance from agent mistakes without expert supervision. For each failed trajectory, a complete failure example (task instruction, initial observation, full action sequence, resulting observations) is given to GPT-4o, which generates 1-4 imperative hints that diagnose the failure and provide generalizable guidance. Hints use placeholders and are typed by task category for retrieval; outputs are strict JSON, normalized, and deduplicated using fuzzy matching with a Levenshtein distance threshold of 0.85. The process yielded 760 ReAct and 650 StateAct hints in ALFWorld, and 756 ReAct and 831 StateAct hints in WebShop after deduplication.
requirements: Failed trajectories from base agent rollouts as input
GPT-4o API access for diagnosis
Prompts enforcing hint length, imperative form, placeholders, and strict JSON output
constraints: Cost depends on the number of failures in the training data, potentially limiting scalability in larger environments
target_learners: LLM agents learning multi-step interactive tasks
target_learning_goals: Avoiding predictable failure modes such as unmet preconditions, redundant commands, and mishandled environment constraints
examples: Example hint: Ensure the {container} is open before attempting to place the {object} inside
key_sources: Humaid Ibrahim, Nikolai Rozanov, Marek Rei. (2025). Fine-Tuning with RAG for Improving LLM Learning of New Skills. ICLR 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01375

article_title: In-Context Function Learning in Large Language Models
citation: Elif Akata, Konstantinos Voudouris, Vincent Fortuin, Eric Schulz. (2026). In-Context Function Learning in Large Language Models. AISTATS 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11863
title: Gaussian-Process-based framework for quantifying and steering LLM inductive biases in continuous function learning
description: The article proposes a unified testbed that casts in-context learning as non-parametric regression under known GP priors. It combines learning-curve evaluation against two references — GP regression as an empirical lower bound and a derived 1-NN rule as a data-driven upper bound — with a likelihood-based inductive-bias analysis: "given a history of demonstrations, we compute the GP posterior predictive distribution under diﬀerent kernel families and record the log-likelihood of the model’s prediction". Aggregating these likelihoods identifies which kernels best explain model behavior, and the resulting bias map is used to target post-training curricula at the kernels under which base models are least consistent.
requirements: Functions must be sampled from known GP kernel families so that posterior predictive likelihoods and reference baselines can be computed
Models must produce parseable numeric predictions at queried inputs
constraints: The likelihood analysis suffers from a variance-inflation problem, meaning predictions are always as or more likely under rougher kernels due to larger variances
Periodic and compositional kernels were treated as beyond scope because they would make the likelihood comparisons less interpretable
It is not yet clear how results generalize from controlled function learning to ecologically valid in-context learning settings
target_learners: Large language models evaluated as in-context learners
target_learning_goals: Continuous function learning from few in-context demonstrations
Steering inductive biases of in-context learners toward desired function classes
examples: Experiment 1 evaluated Qwen-3 8B/14B/32B models on functions from Matérn and SE kernels with length scales 1 and 8, comparing learning curves to GP regression and a 1-NN rule
Experiment 3 fine-tuned low-rank adapters with SFT or GRPO on SE (λ = 8) functions and re-ran the likelihood analysis at 1k, 2k, 5k, and 10k step checkpoints
key_sources: Elif Akata, Konstantinos Voudouris, Vincent Fortuin, Eric Schulz. (2026). In-Context Function Learning in Large Language Models. AISTATS 2026. https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11863
